case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbourline Seafoods (HSL) is a private limited company in the seafood processing sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2008 by Tomas Vale near the coast, it supplies frozen fish to restaurant chains and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership. HSL plans to invest $640,000 in a cold-storage and flash-freezing plant, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit, with an overdraft also available. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.10 a unit and a selling price of $8.10, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. HSL faces spoilage waste of 3.4% and a hygiene certification skills gap among its plant workers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The flash-freezing line packed 15,200 cartons last quarter at a defect rate of 1.5%, down from 2.8% last year. Spoilage waste fell from 6.2% to 3.4% of throughput and delivery to restaurants averages 2.1 days. Market research of 380 chefs found 67% value sustainably sourced fish and 55% would pay $0.35 more per carton. A training review shows 14 of 50 plant workers lack hygiene certification; college certification courses cost $620 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harbourline Seafoods as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.90% to 4.65%, increasing debt-service costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage increases by 6.2% from $12.90 to $13.70 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale fish feed and packaging input costs rose 11.3% year-on-year, while restaurant demand for frozen seafood grew 4.1%.

questions.question_text: HSL plans to fund its $640,000 plant with a $400,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HSL of using retained profit rather than an overdraft to fund the $240,000 portion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is internal cash, so HSL pays no interest and faces no repayable-on-demand clause, unlike an overdraft whose rate would rise with the base rate from 3.90% to 4.65%. With fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $400,000 bank loan already committed, avoiding overdraft interest protects the $4.00 contribution on each of the 70,000 cartons and gives Tomas Vale steadier cash flow while the freezing plant is built.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security and no bank approval, so the $240,000 can be spent quickly on the plant without risking HSL's assets. An overdraft is a short-term facility that the bank could withdraw, leaving the $640,000 project half-finished. Using past profits also keeps control with the existing owners and signals to the bank that the firm is generating enough profit to support its $400,000 loan, which may help when HSL next needs finance.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to HSL, its $640,000 plant and its financing.

questions.question_text: HSL wants to cut spoilage waste of 3.4% on the new line. Consider end-of-line inspection, supplier quality agreements, or staff quality circles. Which should HSL choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
End-of-line inspection: Checking cartons before dispatch would catch defects and remove spoiled fish, protecting the 1.5% defect rate and the promise to restaurants. It is simple to run on the flash-freezing line. However, inspection detects faults only after they occur, so waste has already happened; with 15,200 cartons packed last quarter, a high inspection burden would add labour cost to a firm funding a $640,000 plant.

Supplier quality agreements: Requiring fish suppliers to meet hygiene and freshness standards attacks spoilage at source, which matters because waste fell only from 6.2% to 3.4% and needs to fall further. Cleaner delivered fish also supports the 67% of 380 chefs who value sustainably sourced fish. The drawback is that HSL must monitor suppliers and may pay higher purchase prices, pushing the $4.10 variable cost per unit up and squeezing the $4.00 contribution.

Staff quality circles: Regular groups of the 50 plant workers meeting to solve spoilage problems use their hands-on knowledge, fit the flat structure with democratic leadership, and can identify small fixes that inspection misses. Costs are low and engagement rises. Results are gradual, and the 14 workers without hygiene certification may lack the knowledge to contribute fully at first.

Recommendation: HSL should choose supplier quality agreements. Spoilage originates in the delivered fish, so prevention at source is more effective than end-of-line inspection, which only finds waste after it is created; quality circles are valuable but slower and limited by the certification gap. Supplier agreements can be backed later by quality circles once the 14 workers are certified. The higher purchase cost is justified because it protects the $4.00 contribution on 70,000 units and the $640,000 investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the quality options with minimal application to HSL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in HSL's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why inspection and quality circles are secondary.

questions.question_text: HSL has a flat structure with democratic leadership, but 14 of its 50 plant workers lack hygiene certification and spoilage waste is 3.4%. Explain two benefits for HSL of this leadership and structure in closing the certification gap.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the plant workers to help design the hygiene routines, so the 14 without certification are more likely to attend college courses and apply what they learn. Because the structure is flat, their views reach Tomas Vale quickly without passing through many management layers, speeding decisions that reduce the 3.4% spoilage waste and protect deliveries to restaurants.

Point 2: A flat structure widens each manager's span of control, so experienced workers can coach the 14 trainees directly on the flash-freezing line instead of waiting for a formal hierarchy to arrange it. That supports the 70,000-unit output and helps lower the 1.5% defect rate. Higher involvement also improves morale in a workforce of 50, making it easier to justify the $620 per employee certification cost and to protect the $640,000 plant investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HSL's certification gap, waste and output.

questions.question_text: Fourteen of HSL's 50 workers need hygiene certification. Consider in-house training led by a senior supervisor or external college certification costing $620 per employee. Which should HSL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
In-house training by a senior supervisor: This is tailored to HSL's own flash-freezing line and costs no course fees, and the 14 workers can learn while staying productive, protecting output of 70,000 cartons and the fall in spoilage to 3.4%. It suits the flat structure and democratic leadership. The weakness is that the supervisor's own duties suffer and the training may not lead to the recognised certification that restaurant-chain customers increasingly expect.

External college certification at $620 per worker: A recognised certificate gives the 14 workers formally verified hygiene skills, which supports the 67% of 380 chefs who value sustainably sourced fish and reduces the risk of spoilage complaints. The cost is 14 × $620 = $8,680, small beside the $640,000 plant. The downsides are lost production time while staff attend and generic content that may not cover HSL's specific freezing routines.

Decision: HSL should choose external college certification, followed by short in-house briefings on the plant. The recognised certificate is worth $8,680 because restaurant chains demand proof of hygiene, and in-house training alone cannot supply that; the in-house route is rejected as its certification would not be independently recognised and would divert the supervisor. Short in-house sessions afterwards adapt the college learning to the 15,200-carton line, protecting the $4.00 contribution per unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training options with limited application to HSL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in HSL's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision covering certification, cost and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how the management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($8.10 − $4.10) = $180,000 ÷ $4.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $8.10 − $4.10 = $4.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HSL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with 70,000 cartons produced: the margin of safety is 25,000 units, showing the plant can absorb a demand dip from restaurant chains.
2. Use the $4.00 contribution to test the $0.35 premium the 55% of chefs would pay; a rise from $8.10 to $8.45 lifts contribution to $4.35, which managers can weigh against $180,000 fixed costs.
3. Use unit cost of $6.67 ($180,000 ÷ 70,000 = $2.57 plus $4.10 variable cost) to monitor the 3.4% spoilage waste and target the 1.5% defect rate.
4. Use labour productivity of 1,400 units per worker (70,000 ÷ 50) to judge whether the 14 uncertified workers can be trained without hurting output and whether the $640,000 plant needs more staff.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 25,000-unit margin of safety; $0.35 premium pricing; unit cost $6.67 to cut 3.4% spoilage; labour productivity 1,400 units per worker for staffing.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HSL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HSL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.70 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.90 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $80,000 inventories + $60,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $170,000; 2025 current assets = $100,000 + $70,000 + $55,000 = $225,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $170,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.70; the 2025 comparison is $225,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.80. The stock-excluding measure for 2024 is ($170,000 − $80,000) ÷ $100,000 = $90,000 ÷ $100,000 = 0.90; for 2025 it is ($225,000 − $100,000) ÷ $125,000 = $125,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. Current assets grew from $170,000 to $225,000, faster than current liabilities, which rose from $100,000 to $125,000, so the 2024 figure of 1.70 and 2025 figure of 1.80 show a stronger cushion. The stock-excluding measure rose from 0.90 to 1.00, meaning HSL can now cover every dollar of short-term debt without relying on its $80,000 to $100,000 of inventories — important while it repays a $400,000 bank loan and spends $640,000 on the freezing plant. Cash also rose from $30,000 to $55,000, giving real headroom. The slight concern is that both inventories and trade receivables grew, so some of the improvement is slower-moving stock and unpaid invoices from restaurant chains rather than pure cash; if restaurants delay payment, the 1.00 stock-excluding position could slip below a safe level.

Conclusion: HSL's financial position has improved. Both measures (1.70 to 1.80 and 0.90 to 1.00) are higher, and the rise in cash makes the improvement credible rather than stock-driven. HSL should still watch the growth in receivables while the $640,000 plant is financed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HSL of promoting its fish as sustainably sourced.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The research shows 67% of the 380 chefs value sustainably sourced fish and 55% would pay $0.35 more per carton, so HSL can raise its $8.10 selling price and protect the $4.00 contribution per unit despite an 11.3% rise in fish-feed and packaging costs. It also strengthens relationships with restaurant chains, supporting sales of the 70,000 units needed to justify the $640,000 plant.

Disadvantage: Certified sustainable sourcing can raise the $4.10 variable cost per unit and limit suppliers, which is risky when fish-feed and packaging inputs have already risen 11.3%. If supply is interrupted, the 3.4% spoilage waste could worsen and the 2.1-day delivery promise to restaurants could be missed, damaging the very reputation the claim is meant to build.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HSL's research, costs and plant investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.65%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in fish feed and packaging costs will affect HSL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.90% to 4.65%): If HSL's $400,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). That is small next to fixed costs of $180,000 a year, and a fixed-rate loan would face no increase. Higher rates could cool restaurant demand, but HSL can limit the risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.70 an hour): Some of the workforce of 50 is likely hourly-paid, so wage costs rise. The insert gives no hours worked or role-by-role pay, so no annual wage bill can be invented. The defensible comparison is productivity: 70,000 units ÷ 50 workers = 1,400 units per worker. If the new freezing plant raises output per worker, the wage rise is affordable; if the 14 uncertified workers and 3.4% spoilage hold productivity back, unit labour cost climbs and the $4.00 contribution falls.

Fish feed and packaging input costs (11.3%): These affect the $4.10 variable cost per unit, but the insert does not split it, so only a labelled bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 11.3%, that is 11.3% × $4.10 = about $0.46 per unit; across 70,000 units that is roughly $32,000 a year (70,000 × $0.46). The 55% of chefs willing to pay $0.35 more and 67% valuing sustainable sourcing offer some recovery, but restaurant demand grew only 4.1%, so full pass-through may cost sales.

Conclusion: The 11.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 70,000 units and directly erodes the $4.00 contribution supporting the $640,000 plant; the interest rise is a known $3,000 at most, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity gains from the new plant.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HSL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HSL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
